## 2. Identifying essentials
Prioritizing important expenses first is the core of any financial management system. One way to start is by looking at your tracked expenses and differentiating between essentials and non-essentials. Essentials are the expenses necessary for your daily living, like food, housing and healthcare. Non-essentials are the extra items or services that are less crucial, such as entertainment subscriptions or certain recreational activities.
While essentials are non-negotiable, some strategic planning could help reduce their costs and net potential savings. When it comes to groceries, meal planning around ingredients on sale or minimizing waste from prep work might help get more bang for your buck. For utilities, simple changes like reexamining your water usage habits or investigating your home’s insulation might help save money over time. You may also want to prioritize building an emergency fund to reduce the likelihood of accruing higher-interest debt in the case of a financial emergency.

   Content: ### Steps to building a budget
Use our Budget Builder to help you craft a budget that matches your income and your needs:
1. Build SMART goals: Write a list of what goals you want to accomplish from budgeting. Each goal you supply should be SMART:
- Specific: Be very specific with the goal you're creating (such as, “I want to start building my savings.”)
- Measurable: Provide a number so you can see when you meet a given goal (such as, “I want to have $1200 in my savings account.”)
- Achievable: Goals that you can’t meet will only frustrate you, so be sure to make your goal reachable, given your means (such as, “save $20 from each paycheck.”)
- Relevant: Your goal should be relevant to you (such as, “I want to build savings to prepare for emergencies.”)
